title: Viral Doesn't Pay Rent
summary: I raised $750K and got 30,000 users for a restaurant app that no longer exists — reach is not demand, and the numbers that matter aren't in any platform dashboard.
body_markdown:
I built a restaurant app called Savor. We got to 30,000 users and raised over $750,000. It doesn't exist anymore.


That's the whole lesson in three sentences, and I'd rather lead with it than pretend I learned this from a case study. We had the numbers that look like success on a slide — users, downloads, growth curve, funding — and none of them turned into a business that could pay for itself. I could tell you our user count from memory. I could not have told you what any single one of them was worth.


I bring it up because I hear the restaurant version of that mistake constantly, and it sounds like this: *"our video did 400,000 views."*


Great. How many people ate?


## Reach is not demand


A view is somebody's thumb slowing down for a second. It is not an intention to visit, and on most platforms it isn't even a local person — a video that travels does so by escaping your city, which means the vast majority of that reach can never buy from you.


The uncomfortable version: **a food video that goes viral is often being watched as entertainment by people 900 miles away.** That's not worthless. It just isn't demand, and treating the two as the same number is how operators end up celebrating a week where nothing changed in the till.


The numbers that actually matter are boring and there are only a few:


-


**Views** — New customers who came in that week


-


**Followers** — Phone numbers or emails on your list


-


**Likes** — Repeat rate — did first-timers come back?


-


**Shares** — Revenue vs. the same week last month


-


**"Engagement"** — Cost of the effort vs. dollars it produced


None of the right-hand column is visible in a platform dashboard. All of it is visible in your sales.


## Why this trap is so easy


Because vanity metrics arrive immediately and feel like progress, and revenue arrives slowly and feels like luck.


You post something, and within an hour there's a number going up. It's genuinely satisfying. Meanwhile the actual question — did this produce paying customers — takes weeks to answer and requires you to go look, so most people never close the loop. I didn't, for years, with a company that had a full analytics stack.


There's also a survivorship problem. You see the truck whose video blew up and now has a line. You don't see the hundreds who posted the same kind of video and got nothing, because there's no content about them. Virality is closer to a lottery ticket than a strategy, and strategies are things you can repeat on purpose.


## What actually moved revenue for us


Nothing that scaled. All of it local, small, and unglamorous:


-


**Asking, in person.** The highest-converting marketing I have ever done is a human being asking another human being to do something — join the list, come back Tuesday, try the new thing.


-


**Showing up in the same place on a schedule.** Predictability beats reach for a truck. Being somewhere every Thursday builds a habit; being everywhere once builds nothing.


-


**Owning the contact.** A phone number is worth more than a hundred followers, because you decide when it gets used.


-


**Cross-promoting with a neighbor.** The brewery down the street has your exact customer and no kitchen. That's a free audience with real intent.


-


**Giving regulars something to bring a friend to.** Word of mouth from an existing customer converts at a rate no video will match.


None of that produces a screenshot worth posting. All of it produced money.


## So should you post at all?


Yes — with a different job description for it.


Social media is genuinely good at three things for an independent operator, and none of them are reach:


1.


**Telling existing customers where you are and what's new.** Enormously useful, especially for a truck. This is the real job.


2.


**Being findable and looking alive.** Somebody hears about you and looks you up. A dead account costs you that person. A current one closes them.


3.


**Showing the actual food, well.** Not a trend — the food. People decide to eat with their eyes and this is the cheapest photography budget you'll ever have.


Post for the people who already know you exist. That's it. If something travels beyond them, treat it as weather — pleasant, not repeatable.


## The one thing to do differently this month


Pick your next piece of marketing effort — a post, an event, a promo, whatever — and before you do it, write down the number you expect to move and where you'll check it.


Then actually check it.


That's the whole discipline, and it will change what you spend your time on within two months. Most marketing that operators do has never been measured even once, which means nobody knows which half is working. You can't drop the half that isn't until you look.


## Where the looking gets hard


Here's why people skip the measurement: it's genuinely annoying. Tying "we posted on Tuesday" to "revenue moved on Thursday" means comparing a platform dashboard to a sales report to last month's numbers, by hand, and the effort exceeds the curiosity.


That's the friction we tried to remove. On Avocado your sales, customers, and order history live in one place, so "how did last week compare to the week before," "which customers are new," and "did first-timers come back" are questions you ask in plain language instead of a reconciliation project. Not because the software does your marketing — because it closes the loop fast enough that you'll actually bother.


The numbers I could recite for Savor were the ones our dashboard put in front of me. The ones that would have saved it, I never went looking for. Go look.


*Avocado is a POS built for independent restaurants and food trucks. We help operators make smarter decisions — starting with not wasting money on stuff that doesn't work.*
